## 1. Summary

My preliminary recommendation is **C# / .NET as #1**, with **Go as the strongest #2**, because C# best satisfies the highest-weight AI-coding-automation criterion while also clearing the Azure/Postgres/MCP/observability constraints cleanly. [U] The strongest external evidence so far is that MCP now lists **C#, Go, TypeScript, and Python as Tier 1 SDKs**, while Java and Rust are Tier 2 and Kotlin remains TBD, which removes what would otherwise have been a major Tier 1 uncertainty for C# and Go. [V] ([modelcontextprotocol.io](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/docs/sdk?utm_source=openai)) C# also has a strong Postgres story through Npgsql connection pooling, a mature Azure SDK story through Microsoft’s first-party SDK families, and a mature async/concurrency model for API + worker processes. [V] ([npgsql.org](https://www.npgsql.org/doc/basic-usage.html?utm_source=openai)) Go remains a serious challenger because it has excellent operational simplicity, explicit semantics, fast builds, goroutines, context cancellation, and a now-Tier-1 MCP SDK, but I currently score it behind C# on type-system depth and refactoring safety for AI-driven maintenance. [V][U] ([modelcontextprotocol.io](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/docs/sdk?utm_source=openai))

## 2. My thesis

Choose **C# / .NET** for the Document Verification Service unless the actual engineering team has materially stronger Go expertise or a platform constraint disfavoring .NET in containers. [U] The current ranking I would take into phase 2 is: **1. C# / .NET, 2. Go, 3. Java, 4. TypeScript / Node.js, 5. Kotlin, 6. Rust, 7. Python**. [U]

## 3. Detailed findings

### Research plan for the next phase

I would validate the decision in four passes. [U] First, verify Tier 1 pass/fail for every candidate against **runtime/platform support, Azure SDK coverage, Postgres pooling, MCP server support, OAuth/OIDC, OpenTelemetry, and worker concurrency**. [U] Second, score Tier 2 with extra weight on **2.1 AI-coding-automation fitness**, because the brief explicitly makes that the highest-weight criterion. [U] Third, compare the realistic #1/#2 battle — currently **C# vs Go** — on codegen/refactoring safety, RLS-safe Postgres usage, worker cancellation, schema validation, and operational footprint. [U] Fourth, define flip criteria that would let Go overtake C#, such as a demonstrated internal preference for Go in the platform catalog, a meaningful .NET cold-start/memory problem in Azure Container Apps, or a team-level constraint against .NET. [U]

### Tier 1 preliminary pass/fail

**Platform support:** Azure Container Apps supports containerized applications, and Microsoft’s documentation describes Container Apps as a managed platform for running containerized applications without managing infrastructure. [V] ([learn.microsoft.com](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/container-apps/services?utm_source=openai)) A Container Apps documentation page also says containers can use any runtime, programming language, or development stack of choice, so all seven candidates should be technically deployable if the internal catalog permits their container images. [V] ([learn.microsoft.com](https://learn.microsoft.com/uk-ua/%20azure/container-apps/containers?utm_source=openai)) Azure App Service’s built-in language support is narrower — Microsoft advertises .NET, Node.js, Java, Python, and PHP — but App Service also supports containerized web apps, so App Service should not by itself eliminate Go, Rust, or Kotlin if custom containers are allowed. [V] ([azure.microsoft.com](https://azure.microsoft.com/en-us/solutions/app-service/?utm_source=openai))

**Azure SDKs:** Microsoft’s Azure SDK inventory explicitly covers **.NET, Java, JavaScript/TypeScript, Python, and Go**. [V] ([azure.github.io](https://azure.github.io/azure-sdk/?utm_source=openai)) Microsoft’s Key Vault client-library documentation lists Key Vault client libraries across .NET, Python, Java, JavaScript, and Spring, which supports a strong Tier 1 pass for the main enterprise languages and Java/Kotlin via the JVM ecosystem. [V] ([learn.microsoft.com](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure//key-vault/general/client-libraries?utm_source=openai)) Rust’s Azure SDK position appears to have improved materially: Microsoft Learn documents installing Azure SDK for Rust crates, and the Azure SDK blog announced the Rust SDK as stable on **May 14, 2026**. [V] ([learn.microsoft.com](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/developer/rust/sdk/installation?utm_source=openai)) Kotlin is less clearly first-class as a separate Azure SDK target, but Kotlin/JVM can normally consume Java Azure SDK libraries, so I would treat Kotlin as passing Tier 1 with a caveat rather than eliminating it. [U]

**MCP server library:** The official MCP SDK page lists **TypeScript, Python, C#, and Go as Tier 1 SDKs**, which is highly relevant because the service has an external MCP server surface. [V] ([modelcontextprotocol.io](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/docs/sdk?utm_source=openai)) The same MCP SDK page lists **Java and Rust as Tier 2** and **Kotlin as TBD**, so Java/Rust pass but with lower confidence on maturity, while Kotlin needs either Java SDK interop or a conscious acceptance of lower SDK maturity. [V][U] ([modelcontextprotocol.io](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/docs/sdk?utm_source=openai))

**Postgres pooling and RLS-compatible sessions:** C# has a strong Postgres driver story through Npgsql; Npgsql’s documentation says `NpgsqlDataSource` encapsulates connection configuration and connection pooling, and that data sources are thread-safe and usually correspond to a connection pool. [V] ([npgsql.org](https://www.npgsql.org/doc/basic-usage.html?utm_source=openai)) Go has a strong Postgres story through pgx; pgxpool’s Go package documentation calls it a concurrency-safe connection pool for pgx. [V] ([pkg.go.dev](https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/jackc/pgx/v5/pgxpool?utm_source=openai)) Node has node-postgres, whose documentation says it ships with built-in pooling through `pg-pool`. [V] ([node-postgres.com](https://node-postgres.com/features/pooling?utm_source=openai)) Python has Psycopg 3, whose documentation describes sync and async pool classes that allow many concurrent threads or tasks to use a controlled number of server connections. [V] ([psycopg.org](https://www.psycopg.org/psycopg3/docs/api/pool.html?utm_source=openai)) Java/JVM has JDBC pooling support and mature production poolers such as HikariCP; pgJDBC documentation describes JDBC connection-pooling interfaces and how application code typically acquires pooled connections through `DataSource`. [V] ([jdbc.postgresql.org](https://jdbc.postgresql.org/documentation/datasource/?utm_source=openai)) Rust has SQLx `PgPool`, whose documentation defines `PgPool` as `Pool<Postgres>` and exposes pool acquisition/connection APIs. [V] ([docs.rs](https://docs.rs/sqlx/latest/sqlx/type.PgPool.html?utm_source=openai))

**OpenTelemetry:** OpenTelemetry lists language APIs/SDKs across .NET, JavaScript, Python, Java, Go, Rust, and other languages. [V] ([opentelemetry.io](https://opentelemetry.io/api/?utm_source=openai)) This likely means all candidates pass Tier 1 for instrumentation, but I would still distinguish them in Tier 2.4 because language-specific maturity for logs, metrics, and auto-instrumentation is not identical. [U]

**Concurrency and workers:** Go’s `context` package explicitly carries deadlines and cancellation signals across API boundaries, and its documentation recommends propagating derived contexts with cancel/deadline/timeout through function calls. [V] ([pkg.go.dev](https://pkg.go.dev/context?utm_source=openai)) Microsoft’s .NET stack has mature `async`/`await`, `CancellationToken`, hosted services, and `HttpClient` timeout/cancellation patterns, but I have not yet retrieved a primary Microsoft source for those specifics in this run. [U] Rust/Tokio, Java virtual threads/reactive stacks, Kotlin coroutines, Node async I/O, and Python asyncio can all implement the worker pattern, but their Tier 2 tradeoffs differ more than their Tier 1 feasibility. [U]

### Tier 2 scoring thesis

#### 2.1 — AI-coding-automation fitness

C# is my current winner on 2.1 because it combines rich static typing, nullable-reference annotations, records, interfaces, generics, analyzers, high-quality LSP/Roslyn refactoring, and conventional ASP.NET-style project structure. [U] Those properties matter for AI coding agents because the compiler and analyzer pipeline can catch many mistakes before runtime, and symbol-aware tooling can make large refactors safer. [U] C# is not magic-free — attributes, dependency injection, reflection, serializers, and framework conventions can hide behavior — but the ecosystem’s mainstream conventions are stable enough that AI agents can usually stay inside well-trodden patterns. [U]

Go is the strongest alternative on 2.1 because its formatting, package model, explicit error handling, simple composition model, fast tests, and low implicitness are very friendly to LLM-generated code. [U] The reason I do **not** currently put Go first is that its type system is less expressive than C#, Java/Kotlin, or Rust for modeling domain invariants, and this service has compliance rules, document states, tenant boundaries, and outbox/worker states where richer static modeling can reduce review burden. [U] If the other model argues that Go’s simplicity and deterministic tooling matter more for AI agents than C#’s type-system depth, that is a serious disagreement worth resolving with examples rather than preference. [U]

Java is strong on type safety, refactoring, test tooling, and ecosystem conventions, but I expect it to lose to C# because modern C# has a more concise domain-modeling style and a better ergonomics-to-safety ratio for AI-generated application code. [U] Kotlin has a stronger type system and null-safety story than Java in many respects, but I expect it to lose on lower MCP maturity, more implicit language features, Gradle complexity, and weaker convention uniformity for AI agents. [V][U] ([modelcontextprotocol.io](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/docs/sdk?utm_source=openai)) Rust is excellent on static safety and explicit semantics, but for AI coding agents I expect compile-time lifetime/trait friction and slower iteration to dominate unless the service has unusually high safety/performance requirements. [U] TypeScript has large training-data coverage and frontend alignment, but its type system is structurally unsound in enough common patterns that I would not rank it above C#, Go, or Java for a compliance-heavy modular monolith. [U] Python should pass many ecosystem constraints but should rank last on 2.1 because optional typing and runtime dynamism create a high review burden under AI-driven refactoring. [U]

#### 2.2 — Concurrency model fit

Go is the likely 2.2 winner because goroutines, channels, `context.Context`, and simple worker loops map naturally to the API/outbox/SKIP LOCKED/scheduled-task shape. [V][U] ([pkg.go.dev](https://pkg.go.dev/context?utm_source=openai)) C# is close behind because async/await, cancellation tokens, hosted background services, and mature Postgres pooling are a strong fit for HTTP APIs and worker processes. [U] Java is also strong, especially with modern virtual threads or mature executor/reactive patterns, but JVM memory and cold-start risks are relevant in Azure Container Apps. [U] Node.js is good for high-concurrency I/O but requires more discipline around CPU-bound document parsing and typed worker boundaries. [U] Python can handle the workload with asyncio and worker processes, but runtime typing and packaging/concurrency complexity reduce confidence. [U] Rust can implement the model very well with Tokio and SQLx, but the development-velocity cost is likely not justified for this product’s workload. [V][U] ([docs.rs](https://docs.rs/sqlx/latest/sqlx/type.PgPool.html?utm_source=openai))

#### 2.3 — Ecosystem maturity for the service stack

C# has a very strong ecosystem fit for this service: Npgsql for Postgres pooling, Azure SDKs, OAuth/OIDC middleware, JSON/schema libraries, background-worker patterns, cryptography, structured logging, and enterprise web-service conventions are all mature. [V][U] ([npgsql.org](https://www.npgsql.org/doc/basic-usage.html?utm_source=openai)) Go also has a strong backend ecosystem, and the fact that the official MCP page now lists Go as Tier 1 substantially reduces a previously plausible ecosystem-gap risk. [V][U] ([modelcontextprotocol.io](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/docs/sdk?utm_source=openai)) Java has extremely mature libraries but may carry more framework and runtime complexity than needed for this modular monolith. [U] TypeScript has excellent MCP and schema tooling, but the backend reliability case depends heavily on project discipline around strict typing, runtime validation, and dependency governance. [U] Rust has strong cryptography and systems libraries but a younger Azure/MCP enterprise-app stack than C#, Go, Java, TypeScript, or Python. [V][U] ([devblogs.microsoft.com](https://devblogs.microsoft.com/azure-sdk/from-beta-to-stable-announcing-the-azure-sdk-for-rust-ga/?utm_source=openai)) Python has abundant document-processing and AI-provider ecosystem support, but the brief’s highest-weight criterion penalizes its dynamic nature. [U]

#### 2.4 — Observability and operational fit

Go likely wins operational footprint because it usually produces small static binaries, has low memory overhead, and cold-starts quickly. [U] C# is operationally acceptable and much better than historical .NET Framework stereotypes would suggest, but I would still measure memory and cold start in the actual Azure Container Apps baseline before finalizing HIGH confidence. [U] Java and Kotlin have mature observability ecosystems but carry the JVM cold-start and memory-footprint risk already identified in the brief. [U] Node and Python have acceptable operational profiles for this workload but weaker type/refactoring safety. [U] Rust likely has the best low-level footprint but does not need to win because this service is not primarily CPU- or latency-bound. [U]

### Preliminary ranking

| Rank | Candidate | Preliminary treatment |
|---:|---|---|
| 1 | **C# / .NET** | Best overall balance; current 2.1 winner; strong Azure/Postgres/MCP/OTel fit. [V][U] |
| 2 | **Go** | Best operational/concurrency simplicity; credible #1 alternative; loses narrowly on type-system depth and domain modeling. [V][U] |
| 3 | **Java** | Very mature and safe; likely heavier and less ergonomic than C# for this product. [U] |
| 4 | **TypeScript / Node.js** | Strong MCP/schema/frontend alignment; type-system-depth risk keeps it below C#/Go/Java. [V][U] |
| 5 | **Kotlin** | Strong language, but Kotlin-specific MCP maturity is weaker and JVM/tooling complexity reduces AI-agent predictability. [V][U] |
| 6 | **Rust** | Excellent safety/footprint; too much development-velocity and ecosystem-friction risk for this product. [V][U] |
| 7 | **Python** | Strong ecosystem, but weakest fit for AI-driven large-scale refactoring under this criteria framework. [U] |

### Confidence and flip criteria

My current confidence is **MEDIUM**, because C# and Go are both credible winners and the final answer depends on how heavily we weight C#’s stronger type/refactoring story versus Go’s simpler, more explicit, lower-footprint operational model. [U] The single piece of evidence that would most shift confidence upward would be a small proof-of-concept implementing the same MCP endpoint, RLS-aware Postgres session handling, SKIP LOCKED worker, outbox publisher, OpenTelemetry spans, and schema validation in C# and Go, then comparing AI-agent edit success, test feedback time, code review burden, and runtime footprint. [U]

Go should overtake C# if the proof-of-concept shows materially faster AI-agent iteration with fewer review defects, no meaningful schema/modeling loss from Go’s simpler type system, and clearly better Container Apps memory/cold-start behavior. [U] C# should remain ahead if the proof-of-concept shows safer domain modeling, easier symbol-aware refactoring, cleaner generated tests, and no operational penalty that matters at the expected workload. [U]
